planting.note: Plant a bare-root or container tree in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; self-fertile and needs no second tree to fruit.

directions: Macrocarpa is a trade name used by several specialty fruit nurseries for a large-fruited medlar form, producing noticeably bigger russet-brown fruit, up to two and a half inches across, than a typical seedling medlar on the same small, gnarled, ornamental tree with showy white spring flowers. As with all medlars, the hard fruit is inedible straight off the tree and must be bletted, left in a cool spot for several weeks after the first frosts until it softens and darkens into a spiced, wine-like pulp suited to jelly or eating fresh as a confection. The tree tolerates poor soils and needs little pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood, cropping best in a sheltered, sunny spot where the early spring blossom escapes late frost damage. Harvest once the fruit has colored fully and the calyx end opens, then set it aside to finish ripening before use.

planting.note: Plant a bare-root or container tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; self-fertile and tolerant of colder sites than many Western European medlar selections.

directions: Russian medlar is an old large-fruited selection, distinct from the standard seedling medlar mainly in the size of its fruit. The small, twisting tree carries the species' usual showy white spring flowers before setting hard, russet fruit that must be bletted after a hard frost, softening over several weeks in cool storage into a rich, spiced pulp used for jelly, sauces, or eating fresh. It needs no second tree for pollination, tolerates lean or poor soils, and requires only light pruning to remove dead or crossing wood. Harvest after the first good frost and let the fruit finish softening indoors before use.

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; self-fertile and needs no second tree.

directions: Chelsea, also sold under the synonym King James, is an RHS Award of Garden Merit black mulberry propagated from cuttings of a historic tree at what is now the Chelsea Physic Garden in London, grown for the species' characteristically dark, sweet-tart, blackberry-like fruit on a gnarled, long-lived, broadly spreading tree. It leafs out late in spring, so late frosts rarely damage new growth, and fruit ripens over several weeks in mid to late summer rather than all at once, which stretches out the harvest but also means ripe berries drop and stain paving below. The tree is self-fertile, slow to reach full size, and largely trouble-free once established in deep, well-drained soil. Site it away from paths and patios where falling fruit will be a nuisance, and pick berries by shaking ripe clusters onto a tarp rather than hand-picking, since fully ripe fruit bruises easily.

planting.note: Plant a container tree in spring after frost danger passes, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this compact selection fruits well even in a large patio pot.

directions: Thai Dwarf is a naturally compact, heavy-bearing tropical mulberry selection popular with backyard growers in warm climates for producing an outsized crop of elongated, sweet berries on a small, manageable tree or large shrub. Unlike temperate mulberries it fruits nearly continuously through the warm season rather than in one concentrated flush, and young plants can begin cropping within their first year or two. It is self-fertile, roots readily from cuttings, and performs well in containers where winters are too cold for in-ground planting, needing to be moved under cover below the high 20s F. Keep soil consistently moist and feed lightly through the growing season for the heaviest, best-flavored harvest.
